subject: Issues with vectorised Bernoulli in Jolly-Seber with per-capita recruitment

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Issues with vectorised Bernoulli in Jolly-Seber with per-capita recruitment
parts:
Hi all,

I wrapped my head around parameterising the removal entry probability in Jolly-Seber models as a function of the per-capita recruitment rate (f), population size (N), and number of available recruits (A), to be able to place a prior directly on f. However, this model runs very slowly leading me to want to vectorise to speed things up. My attempt at the vectorised Bernoulli is as follows:

dbern_vec <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1), prob = double(1), log = integer(0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dbinom(x = x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
    return(logProb)
  }
)

The likelihood of the (non-vectorised) model, including f as function of N and A, is as follows:

# Recruitment
psi[1] ~ dbeta(1, 1)                    # Nuisance parameter
for (t in 2:n.occ) {
   f[t-1] ~ dexp(1)                        # Per-capita recruitment
   psi[t] <- f[t-1] * N[t-1] / A[t-1]  # Removal entry probability
}
for (i in 1:n.ind) {
   z[i,1] ~ dbern(psi[1])                                         # Entry first occasion (nuisance)
   a[i,1] <- 1 - z[i,1]                                                  # Recruitable individuals
   for (t in 2:n.occ) {
      z[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t-1] * phi + a[i,t-1] * psi[t])  # Survival and recruitment
      a[i,t] <- a[i,t-1] * (1 - z[i,t])                                # Recruitable individuals
   } # t
   for (t in 1:n.occ) {
      y[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t] * p)
   } # t 
} # i
for (t in 1:n.occ) {       
   N[t] <- sum(z[1:n.ind,t])  # Population size per occasion    
   A[t] <- sum(a[1:n.ind,t])  # Recruitable individuals per occasion   
 }

Now, the vectorised version works only if the simulated z values are used as initial values, and even then N and A don't change their values. I think there's an issue with samplers getting assigned to z, but I'm not sure. Did I make an error with the vectorised Bernoulli, or is there an issue with using the derived variables in the vectorised likelihood?

I've attached a reproducible script to simulate and analyse the capture histories with both the vectorised and non-vectorised model. I'd love to hear where I went wrong, because I plan to use this model for a large, multisite dataset.

Sincerely,

Matt

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Issues with vectorised Bernoulli in Jolly-Seber with per-capita recruitment
parts:
Matt, good question.  You're exactly right that this has to do with sampler assignment.

Fundamentally, what's going wrong here is that nimble doesn't know that your (custom-written) dbern_vec multivariate distribution is a *discrete* distribution, in this case only allowing values of 0 and 1.  When nimble performs default sampler assignment (for your vectorized "m1" model), since nimble doesn't contain any other _multivariate discrete_ distributions, the default sampler assignment for multivariate distributions, in the absence of conjugacy, is the RW_block sampler (multivariate Metropolis-Hastings sampling, with a multivariate normal proposal distribution - designed for continuous-valued multivariate distributions).  You can see this in the output from your code:

> m1conf <- configureMCMC(m1model, monitors = m1mons)
## ===== Monitors =====
## thin = 1: A, f, N, p, phi
## ===== Samplers =====
## RW_block sampler (8)
##   - z[]  (8 multivariate elements)
## RW sampler (10)
##   - phi
##   - p
##   - psi.alpha
##   - f[]  (7 elements)

Or more explicitly, as:

> m1conf$printSamplers('z')
## [11] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 1]
## [12] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 2]
## [13] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 3]
## [14] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 4]
## [15] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 5]
## [16] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 6]
## [17] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 7]
## [18] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 8]

This (silently) fails to sample, because none of the continuous-valued proposals for changes to elements of z[1:400, t] are ever accepted, thus the posteriors failing to transition.

Vectorisation requires some careful thought, at the very least, regarding when it will / won't lead to gains in efficiency.  We always suggest: "think about the model graph".  For the likelihood, y, the vectorised declaration does the following: y[1:n.ind,t] is declared as a *single* multivariate node.  If the elements of z[i,t] are declared as scalars, then each update to any element z[i,t] will require calculating the likelihood of the entire vector y[1:n.ind,t].  So this will be a huge additional computational cost, and won't improve things.  So we wouldn't want to vectorize the likelihood, unless each z[1:n.ind,t] is also defined as a vectorised multivariate node - as you tried to do (in which case, the multivariate update to each z[1:n.ind,t] would require calculation of the full likelihood of y[1:n.ind,t] anyway, so there is no additional computation, but only a more streamlined model structure).

So, if we have a good way to sample the latent _discrete multivariate_ z[1:n.ind,t] terms, then we might consider this approach.  That said, with n.ind = 200+200 = 400, any 400-dimensional multivariate sampler is going to struggle immensely to update such a high-dimensional variable.  So even if we had a mechanism for doing this (for example, the AF_slice sampler), I don't imagine it would lead to any gains in efficiency.

So, going back to your non-vectorised (m2) model.  Towards the end of improving efficiency, my suspicion is that sampling of the z[i,t] terms, due to the extensive dependency chains (propagating through N, a, A, psi, and ultimately a slew of other z[i,t] terms) is slowing things down a lot.  That said, you can check *where* the MCMC sampling time is going to, using the core mcmc$run method (instead of runMCMC) as:

m1mcmc$run(niter, time = TRUE)
m1mcmc$getTimes()

See the very brief section 7.5.2 "Measuring sampler computation times: getTimes" of the User Manual.  This partitions the total sampling time _by sampler_, so you can see which samplers are taking the majority of the time.

As for improving this; I suspect some amount of unnecessary computation could be avoided through some clever thinking about dependencies, and perhaps some use of custom-written functions, or otherwise, but this would be another undertaking.  I have not started that thought process, but such undertakings alway pan out to be deep (and rewarding) mental dives.

I hope this helps somewhat.  I'm sorry I don't have concrete suggestions for improvement right now, but I at least wanted to clarify what the problem is.  Keep in touch with questions.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Issues with vectorised Bernoulli in Jolly-Seber with per-capita recruitment
parts:
InHi Matt,

I'll chime in here too.  Any time a sampler updates a node, it will need to calculate the stochastic dependencies, i.e. log probabilities, (and deterministic dependencies that come first) one or more times (depending on how many possible updated values the sampler considers, which depends on the kind of sampler).  In your model structure (aka graph), any time a sampler updates z[i, t], the calculations will include a[i, t], hence a[i, t+1]... a[i, n.occ], hence A[t]...A[t.occ], hence psi[t+1]...psi[n.occ], hence z[i, t+1]... z[i, n.occ] for all i, if I follow.  So it looks like the bookkeeping for psi[t] means that calculations for every latent state for all individuals at all times past t must be done when updating any z[i, t].  This would be an enormous dependency structure that could bog down any MCMC.  

In a case like this, we look for places where the same model can be represented equivalently but with different stochastic and deterministic relationships.  A canonical example is a basic state-space model, where options A and B below are equivalent but option A is computationally enormously inefficient.

Option A:
# ignore initial state declarations and priors
for(t in 2:1000) {
   eps[t] ~ dnorm(0, sd = process_sigma)
   state[t] <- a + b*state[t-1] + eps[t]
   observation[t] ~ dnorm(state[t], sd = observation_sigma)
}

Option B:
# ignore initial state declarations and priors
for(t in 2:1000) {
   state[t] ~ dnorm(a + b*state[t-1], sd = process_sigma)
   observation[t] ~ dnorm(state[t], sd = observation_sigma)
}

To sample state[t] in option A, all state[t]...state[1000] and observation[t]...observation[1000] must be calculated.  This means the computational burden for the samplers increases quadratically with the length of the series (1000 in this case). To sample state[t] in option B, only state[t], state[t+1], and observation[t] must be calculated.  (Calculate here means a log probability for a stochastic node.). This means the computational burden increases only linearly with the length of the series. 

Back to your case.  One idea I see would be to replace

f[t-1] ~ dexp(1)                        # Per-capita recruitment
psi[t] <- f[t-1] * N[t-1] / A[t-1]  # Removal entry probability

with

psi[t] ~ drecruit(N[t-1] / A[t-1])

where you could write drecruit to calculate f from psi and N[t-1]/A[t-1] and then calculate and return the (log) dexp value for that f.  Now, when a sampler considers a different value for z[i,t], the dependency chain will stop at psi[t] (rather than continuing on to the entire rest of z[i, t] for all later values of t).  Rather than having f[t] stochastic and psi[t] calculated from f[t], you will have psi[t] itself stochastic.  I haven't run your code and experimented, but it looks like this kind of change might help.  I haven't thought as much about the intertwined z[i,t] and a[i, t] steps.

Another option would be to write custom samplers that take advantage of the specific structure of this model, but that would be somewhat more involved.

HTH
Perry

parts:
Hi Perry and Daniel,

As per usual the feedback has been great! I think I will stay away from the vectorised distribution and look for an HPC to run this model. Because it gets more complicated than this: I'm particularly interested in temporal correlations between f and phi, and we have data from 60< sites: so we have a bivariate structure for f and phi, where the means, SDs, and correlation coefficients are going to be hierarchically modeled across sites. Add to this the data augmentation required and we've got a proper mega-model.

If possible, I'd just like to clear a few things up from the things you've said:
  1. Use fewer intermediate nodes. Does this also mean that NOT calculating N[t] and A[t] as derived quantities but doing it directly in the declaration for psi[t], i.e., psi[t] <- f[t-1] * sum(z[1:n.ind,t]) / sum(a[1:n.ind,t]), would speed up the model? Or is this not analogous to your Option A and B above, Perry?
  2. Probably not use non-centered parameterisation for random effects?
  3. Would it still be possible to do something similar to the drecruit() line above if I need to model f and phi and multivariate?
Thanks again!

Regards,

Matt

##   - z[]  (8 multivariate elements)
## RW sampler (10)
##   - phi
##   - p
##   - psi.alpha
##   - f[]  (7 elements)

Or more explicitly, as:

> m1conf$printSamplers('z')
## [11] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 1]
## [12] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 2]
## [13] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 3]
## [14] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 4]
## [15] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 5]
## [16] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 6]
## [17] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 7]
## [18] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 8]

This (silently) fails to sample, because none of the continuous-valued proposals for changes to elements of z[1:400, t] are ever accepted, thus the posteriors failing to transition.

Vectorisation requires some careful thought, at the very least, regarding when it will / won't lead to gains in efficiency.  We always suggest: "think about the model graph".  For the likelihood, y, the vectorised declaration does the following: y[1:n.ind,t] is declared as a *single* multivariate node.  If the elements of z[i,t] are declared as scalars, then each update to any element z[i,t] will require calculating the likelihood of the entire vector y[1:n.ind,t].  So this will be a huge additional computational cost, and won't improve things.  So we wouldn't want to vectorize the likelihood, unless each z[1:n.ind,t] is also defined as a vectorised multivariate node - as you tried to do (in which case, the multivariate update to each z[1:n.ind,t] would require calculation of the full likelihood of y[1:n.ind,t] anyway, so there is no additional computation, but only a more streamlined model structure).

So, if we have a good way to sample the latent _discrete multivariate_ z[1:n.ind,t] terms, then we might consider this approach.  That said, with n.ind = 200+200 = 400, any 400-dimensional multivariate sampler is going to struggle immensely to update such a high-dimensional variable.  So even if we had a mechanism for doing this (for example, the AF_slice sampler), I don't imagine it would lead to any gains in efficiency.

So, going back to your non-vectorised (m2) model.  Towards the end of improving efficiency, my suspicion is that sampling of the z[i,t] terms, due to the extensive dependency chains (propagating through N, a, A, psi, and ultimately a slew of other z[i,t] terms) is slowing things down a lot.  That said, you can check *where* the MCMC sampling time is going to, using the core mcmc$run method (instead of runMCMC) as:

m1mcmc$run(niter, time = TRUE)
m1mcmc$getTimes()

See the very brief section 7.5.2 "Measuring sampler computation times: getTimes" of the User Manual.  This partitions the total sampling time _by sampler_, so you can see which samplers are taking the majority of the time.

As for improving this; I suspect some amount of unnecessary computation could be avoided through some clever thinking about dependencies, and perhaps some use of custom-written functions, or otherwise, but this would be another undertaking.  I have not started that thought process, but such undertakings alway pan out to be deep (and rewarding) mental dives.

I hope this helps somewhat.  I'm sorry I don't have concrete suggestions for improvement right now, but I at least wanted to clarify what the problem is.  Keep in touch with questions.

Cheers,
Daniel





On Mon, Oct 31, 2022 at 6:46 PM Matthijs Hollanders <matthijs....@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi all,

I wrapped my head around parameterising the removal entry probability in Jolly-Seber models as a function of the per-capita recruitment rate (f), population size (N), and number of available recruits (A), to be able to place a prior directly on f. However, this model runs very slowly leading me to want to vectorise to speed things up. My attempt at the vectorised Bernoulli is as follows:

dbern_vec <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1), prob = double(1), log = integer(0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dbinom(x = x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
    return(logProb)
  }
)

The likelihood of the (non-vectorised) model, including f as function of N and A, is as follows:

# Recruitment
psi[1] ~ dbeta(1, 1)                    # Nuisance parameter
for (t in 2:n.occ) {
   f[t-1] ~ dexp(1)                        # Per-capita recruitment
   psi[t] <- f[t-1] * N[t-1] / A[t-1]  # Removal entry probability
}
for (i in 1:n.ind) {
   z[i,1] ~ dbern(psi[1])                                         # Entry first occasion (nuisance)
   a[i,1] <- 1 - z[i,1]                                                  # Recruitable individuals
   for (t in 2:n.occ) {
      z[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t-1] * phi + a[i,t-1] * psi[t])  # Survival and recruitment
      a[i,t] <- a[i,t-1] * (1 - z[i,t])                                # Recruitable individuals
   } # t
   for (t in 1:n.occ) {
      y[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t] * p)
   } # t 
} # i
for (t in 1:n.occ) {       
   N[t] <- sum(z[1:n.ind,t])  # Population size per occasion    
   A[t] <- sum(a[1:n.ind,t])  # Recruitable individuals per occasion   
 }

Now, the vectorised version works only if the simulated z values are used as initial values, and even then N and A don't change their values. I think there's an issue with samplers getting assigned to z, but I'm not sure. Did I make an error with the vectorised Bernoulli, or is there an issue with using the derived variables in the vectorised likelihood?

I've attached a reproducible script to simulate and analyse the capture histories with both the vectorised and non-vectorised model. I'd love to hear where I went wrong, because I plan to use this model for a large, multisite dataset.

Sincerely,

Matt

parts:
Hi Matt,

Thanks for the follow-ups.  The key point is not about using fewer intermediate nodes (although that can help, but it's a separate kind of issue) but rather breaking the long chain of deterministic dependencies by making one of them a stochastic dependency.  This relates to centered vs non-centered parameterizations, as you say, although in the case of your f[t] that terminology is a bit mislabeled even though the basic issue is the same.

A good way to see what is going on would be to check dependencies.  After you build the model, try

model$getDependencies("z[10, 3]") # or whatever i and t you want.

This will return the nodes needing calculation every time z[10, 3] is updated.  If you change things to make psi[t] the stochastic node, and then go through these steps, I think you will see much smaller dependencies.

Yes, you could do it in a multivariate way.  In the univariate case, a way to see that the models are equivalent is that (doing math here, not code)

pdf(f[t]) = exp(-f[t]) # your prior: exp(1) # I am using pdf(x) for the probability density function of x, since here you have a variable called "f" :-)

psi[t] = f[t-1] * C # where C = N[t-1] / A[t-1]. # psi[t] is a function of the random variable f[t-1]

pdf(psi[t]) = pdf( psi[t] / C) / C # Using probability theory for the distribution of a function of a random variable, this is the pdf of psi[t]

So you could write a user-defined distribution for psi[t] that returns the log probability density as 

-psi[t] / C - log(C)

and this would result in an equivalent model to what you have.

(This is slightly different from what I wrote more hastily yesterday).

Again, if you have psi[t] as the random variable instead of f[t], then a change in A[t] will require a new log probability value for psi[t] but the psi[t] value itself will not change so calculations that depend on it will not need to be done.

In a multivariate case, I think you would have multivariate f[1:T], and psi[1:T] as a function of f[1:T], and you could write a multivariate distribution for psi[1:T] derived from whatever you want the multivariate prior for f[1:T] to be (which I see on Twitter you are generating ideas for ;-) ).  

Perry

On Wed, Nov 2, 2022 at 11:12 AM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
InHi Matt,

I'll chime in here too.  Any time a sampler updates a node, it will need to calculate the stochastic dependencies, i.e. log probabilities, (and deterministic dependencies that come first) one or more times (depending on how many possible updated values the sampler considers, which depends on the kind of sampler).  In your model structure (aka graph), any time a sampler updates z[i, t], the calculations will include a[i, t], hence a[i, t+1]... a[i, n.occ], hence A[t]...A[t.occ], hence psi[t+1]...psi[n.occ], hence z[i, t+1]... z[i, n.occ] for all i, if I follow.  So it looks like the bookkeeping for psi[t] means that calculations for every latent state for all individuals at all times past t must be done when updating any z[i, t].  This would be an enormous dependency structure that could bog down any MCMC.  

In a case like this, we look for places where the same model can be represented equivalently but with different stochastic and deterministic relationships.  A canonical example is a basic state-space model, where options A and B below are equivalent but option A is computationally enormously inefficient.

Option A:
# ignore initial state declarations and priors
for(t in 2:1000) {
   eps[t] ~ dnorm(0, sd = process_sigma)
   state[t] <- a + b*state[t-1] + eps[t]
   observation[t] ~ dnorm(state[t], sd = observation_sigma)
}

Option B:
# ignore initial state declarations and priors
for(t in 2:1000) {
   state[t] ~ dnorm(a + b*state[t-1], sd = process_sigma)
   observation[t] ~ dnorm(state[t], sd = observation_sigma)
}

To sample state[t] in option A, all state[t]...state[1000] and observation[t]...observation[1000] must be calculated.  This means the computational burden for the samplers increases quadratically with the length of the series (1000 in this case). To sample state[t] in option B, only state[t], state[t+1], and observation[t] must be calculated.  (Calculate here means a log probability for a stochastic node.). This means the computational burden increases only linearly with the length of the series. 

Back to your case.  One idea I see would be to replace

f[t-1] ~ dexp(1)                        # Per-capita recruitment
psi[t] <- f[t-1] * N[t-1] / A[t-1]  # Removal entry probability

with

psi[t] ~ drecruit(N[t-1] / A[t-1])

where you could write drecruit to calculate f from psi and N[t-1]/A[t-1] and then calculate and return the (log) dexp value for that f.  Now, when a sampler considers a different value for z[i,t], the dependency chain will stop at psi[t] (rather than continuing on to the entire rest of z[i, t] for all later values of t).  Rather than having f[t] stochastic and psi[t] calculated from f[t], you will have psi[t] itself stochastic.  I haven't run your code and experimented, but it looks like this kind of change might help.  I haven't thought as much about the intertwined z[i,t] and a[i, t] steps.

Another option would be to write custom samplers that take advantage of the specific structure of this model, but that would be somewhat more involved.

HTH
Perry

## thin = 1: A, f, N, p, phi
## ===== Samplers =====
## RW_block sampler (8)

## RW sampler (10)
##   - phi
##   - p
##   - psi.alpha
##   - f[]  (7 elements)

## [13] RW_block sampler: z[1:400, 3]
